The integrator's DC gain (20.66 dB ≈ 20·log10(Rl/R1) = 20.8 dB) and the output offset are consistent with the netlist, so the feedback resistors are not the problem. The unity-gain frequency is far off target. Nominal R1·Cf gives about 4.2 MHz, and the measured 22.9 MHz is well above the 2.68–3.28 MHz window. The slope is also flatter than -20 dB/dec. The most likely culprit is Cf, since a smaller-than-intended integrating capacitor pushes the crossover up. Cc is the next candidate because it sets the op-amp dominant pole and can distort the rolloff. R1 is the third.

```json
{"ranking": ["Cf", "Cc", "R1"], "fault": "Integrating feedback capacitor Cf appears wrong (2.814 pF, too small). Since f_unity ~ 1/(2*pi*R1*Cf), the smaller value pushes the unity-gain crossover to about 22.9 MHz instead of about 3 MHz, and the flattened slope (-14.8 dB/dec) indicates the op-amp's own compensation (Cc/Rz, GBW) is also interacting with the loop. Restoring Cf to roughly 4 pF (for R1 = 13.3k) should bring f_unity into the target band."}
```
